blocks.text: Pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an aerobic, acid-fast bacillus transmitted primarily through inhalation of airborne droplet nuclei from a person with infectious pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis.
The organism primarily affects the lungs but may spread through the bloodstream or lymphatics to other organs.
A. Based on anatomical site

items.text: Pulmonary tuberculosis: involving the lung parenchyma, tracheobronchial tree or larynx.
Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB): involving organs outside the lungs, e.g. lymph nodes, pleura, meninges, bones, kidneys and gastrointestinal tract.
Disseminated/miliary tuberculosis: widespread haematogenous dissemination involving multiple organs.

blocks.text: B. Based on previous treatment history

rows: Never treated for TB or received anti-TB drugs for less than one month
Previously treated, declared cured or treatment completed, now diagnosed again
Previously treated but interrupted treatment and subsequently returned
Previously treated, but outcome is unknown or does not fit the above categories

blocks.text: C. Based on drug susceptibility

rows: Susceptible to the relevant first-line anti-TB drugs
Resistant to isoniazid but not meeting MDR-TB criteria
Resistant to rifampicin, with or without resistance to other drugs
Resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin
MDR/RR-TB with additional resistance to any fluoroquinolone
MDR/RR-TB with resistance to any fluoroquinolone and at least one additional Group A drug (bedaquiline or linezolid)

blocks.text: Important: Treatment history and drug-resistance classification must not be confused. A patient with recurrent TB does not automatically have MDR-TB.
Unlike hypertension or asthma, pulmonary TB does not have one universally adopted numerical severity-grading system for routine treatment selection.
For practical prescribing, classify disease as follows:

rows: Limited, non-cavitary pulmonary disease; low bacillary burden; no major complications
More extensive pulmonary involvement, significant symptoms or cavitation
Extensive bilateral disease, respiratory compromise, major haemoptysis, severe hypoxaemia or disseminated disease

blocks.text: This is a practical clinical description, not a formal WHO staging system. Drug susceptibility, anatomical site, HIV status and previous treatment are more important in selecting the regimen.
The diagnosis of pulmonary TB should ideally be bacteriologically confirmed before treatment.

blocks.text: Important prescribing principle: A patient with a positive Xpert MTB result and rifampicin resistance should not simply be placed on the standard first-line regimen while awaiting prolonged treatment response. The patient requires prompt drug-resistance evaluation and referral into the appropriate TB programme.

blocks.text: Uncomplicated pulmonary TB is generally managed with outpatient multidrug therapy.

blocks.title: Hospital admission and immediate supportive treatment may be required in patients with:

items.text: Severe malnutrition or inability to take oral medication.
Major complications or significant drug toxicity.
Management of haemoptysis and other complications.

blocks.text: Infection prevention: Suspected or confirmed infectious pulmonary TB requires airborne precautions, adequate ventilation, appropriate respiratory protection for healthcare workers and a well-fitting medical mask for the patient when being transported.
The standard WHO-recommended regimen is a six-month, daily, four-drug followed by two-drug regimen.
Total duration: 6 months
Intensive phase — 2 months
Continuation phase — 4 months
All medicines are administered once daily. The standard regimen is supported by WHO recommendations and is used in national TB programmes.
Rationale for the four drugs

rows: Bactericidal and sterilising activity against different bacterial populations
Acts particularly against bacilli in acidic environments
Helps prevent selection of resistant organisms during initial therapy

blocks.text: The intensive phase rapidly reduces the bacterial burden, while the continuation phase eliminates persisting organisms and reduces relapse.
**4.2 Alternative shorter regimens**
WHO recognises shorter regimens for selected patients. They are not interchangeable with the standard regimen without checking eligibility and national programme implementation.
A. Four-month rifapentine-based regimen

blocks.text: Written as:
[ 2HPZM/2HPM ]

For eligible children aged 3 months to under 16 years:

items.text: Intensive phase: 2 months HRZ, with ethambutol where indicated.

blocks.text: Non-severe disease includes uncomplicated pleural effusion and selected limited, non-cavitary pulmonary disease.
Children with severe pulmonary disease, miliary TB or other severe forms should not automatically receive this shortened regimen.
**4.3 Drug-resistant pulmonary TB**
Drug-resistant TB requires a different regimen and specialist/National TB Programme management.

rows: Rifampicin-based regimen with additional drugs, commonly including levofloxacin

blocks.text: Important: Do not add a single drug to a failing regimen. This can result in further resistance.

**5.3 Prescription example: adult weighing 60 kg**
For a patient with newly diagnosed, drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, eligible for the standard six-month regimen:
Prescription 1 – Intensive phase

items.text: Tablet rifampicin 150 mg + isoniazid 75 mg + pyrazinamide 400 mg + ethambutol 275 mg.
Take 4 tablets orally once daily for 2 months.

blocks.text: Prescription 2 – Continuation phase

items.text: Take 4 tablets orally once daily for 4 months.

blocks.text: This illustrates a common adult FDC strength and dosing approach. The actual number of tablets must be checked against the current NTBLCP weight-band chart and the formulation supplied. National TB programme dispensing schedules may use different pack sizes and dispensing intervals.
**5.4 Pyridoxine supplementation**
Isoniazid can cause peripheral neuropathy by interfering with pyridoxine metabolism.

items.text: Tablet pyridoxine 25–50 mg orally once daily during isoniazid therapy, particularly in patients at increased risk.

blocks.text: Higher doses may be required in selected patients under specialist guidance. Avoid unnecessary prolonged high-dose pyridoxine because it can itself cause sensory neuropathy.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Adverse effects, complications and toxicity management

content_groups.group_title: 9.1 Important adverse effects of first-line drugs

rows: Hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, haemolysis, acute kidney injury

content_groups.group_title: 9.2 Recognition and management of important toxicities

blocks.text: A. Drug-induced liver injury (DILI)

blocks.title: Diagnostic criteria commonly used to identify significant anti-TB drug-induced liver injury:

items.text: ALT at least 3 times the upper limit of normal with symptoms of hepatitis; OR
ALT at least 5 times the upper limit of normal without symptoms.
Stop the hepatotoxic TB medicines when the above thresholds are met.
Assess liver function, bilirubin and coagulation.
Exclude alternative causes, including viral hepatitis and other hepatotoxic drugs.
Once liver enzymes have sufficiently improved, reintroduce essential medicines using an appropriate sequential rechallenge protocol.
If severe hepatitis occurs, an alternative regimen may be needed.

blocks.text: Do not simply continue all hepatotoxic drugs in a patient with clinically significant hepatitis.
B. Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy

items.text: Assess for other causes of neuropathy.
Severe or progressive symptoms require specialist review and consideration of isoniazid modification.

blocks.text: C. Ethambutol-induced optic neuritis

items.text: Stop ethambutol immediately if optic toxicity is suspected.
Review the TB regimen to ensure adequate active drug coverage.
Do not restart ethambutol without specialist assessment.

blocks.text: D. Rifampicin-induced thrombocytopenia

items.text: Stop rifampicin immediately if immune-mediated thrombocytopenia is suspected.
Avoid rifampicin rechallenge in confirmed immune-mediated thrombocytopenia.

blocks.text: E. Pyrazinamide-induced hyperuricaemia

items.text: Check uric acid if clinically indicated.
Manage symptomatic gout using an appropriate anti-inflammatory regimen, considering renal and hepatic function.
Persistent severe toxicity may require specialist review of the TB regimen.

blocks.text: Monitoring is essential to establish treatment effectiveness, detect adverse effects and prevent the emergence of drug resistance.
Before initiating treatment, document:

rows: Establishes bacteriological diagnosis and rifampicin resistance

blocks.text: Not every patient requires every laboratory investigation repeated routinely. Monitoring should be guided by baseline abnormalities, comorbidities and symptoms.

rows: Clinical status, weight, sputum bacteriology, HIV status and relevant laboratory investigations
Weight, adherence, adverse effects, symptoms and treatment response
Sputum bacteriology where initially bacteriologically positive; assess response and continuation-phase dosing
Sputum bacteriology and assessment for treatment failure
End-of-treatment evaluation and final sputum bacteriology according to programme protocol

blocks.text: In bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB, sputum conversion is an important treatment-response marker.
Radiological improvement may lag behind clinical and bacteriological improvement.

blocks.title: Treatment failure should be suspected when:

items.text: Sputum remains positive or becomes positive again at month 5 or later during treatment.
Symptoms persist or worsen despite adequate treatment.
There is clinical deterioration or new radiological progression.
There is evidence of drug resistance or inadequate drug exposure.
Review adherence and actual drug doses.
Check whether the patient has been receiving the correct weight-band formulation.
Assess for malabsorption and drug interactions.
Repeat molecular testing and obtain culture/DST as indicated.
Assess for HIV, diabetes and other comorbidities.
Refer to the drug-resistant TB treatment service where indicated.

blocks.text: Do not empirically restart the same regimen or add a single drug to a failing regimen.
The decision to continue, restart or modify treatment depends on the interruption pattern and national TB programme guidance.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Discharge counselling, follow-up and clinical pearls

blocks.text: Patients should be counselled on the following:
Medication adherence

items.text: Take medications every day as prescribed.
Complete the entire treatment course even if symptoms resolve.
Do not stop medication when the cough disappears.
Do not share TB medications with another person.
Report missed doses and adverse effects promptly.

blocks.text: Infection prevention

items.text: Avoid crowded, poorly ventilated environments during the infectious period.
Use a medical mask when advised, particularly in shared indoor spaces.
Household contacts should be evaluated through contact investigation.

blocks.text: Nutrition

items.text: Maintain adequate calorie and protein intake.
Avoid excessive alcohol consumption because of the risk of hepatotoxicity.
Stop smoking and avoid exposure to indoor air pollution.

items.text: Rifampicin is the most important drug for sterilising activity and prevention of relapse.
Isoniazid is associated with peripheral neuropathy; pyridoxine helps prevent it.
Rifampicin causes orange-red discolouration of body fluids.
Pyrazinamide is associated with hyperuricaemia and hepatotoxicity.
Ethambutol can cause optic neuritis and red-green colour discrimination defects.
Never use rifampicin or isoniazid as monotherapy for active TB.
A negative sputum smear does not exclude pulmonary TB.
Xpert MTB/RIF detects TB and rifampicin resistance but does not establish susceptibility to every anti-TB drug.
A patient with rifampicin-resistant TB needs evaluation for MDR/RR-TB.
Always reassess drug doses when the patient's weight changes.
Persistent sputum positivity requires investigation for resistance, non-adherence and inadequate drug exposure.
Patients with TB should be screened for HIV and diabetes.
TB treatment is not routinely discontinued simply because the patient becomes asymptomatic.
Drug-resistant TB must be treated using an appropriate combination of active medicines, not by adding one drug to a failing regimen.

blocks.text: Prescribing update: The September 2026 WHO guideline is newer than the 2025 operational handbook. Its updated recommendations, especially for drug-resistant TB, should take precedence where they differ from older guidance. National programme implementation and availability must also be considered.
